column2: Our drawing rule asks for a function whose derivative equals itself, starting at one. Try a polynomial. Put its coefficients in boxes, one box for each power. Differentiation moves each term one column left and multiplies its coefficient by the power it came from. To make the two rows agree, what must the coefficient of x be?

It must be one. Now the derivative of b times x squared is two b times x. That must match the x term above, whose coefficient is one. So b is one half. The derivative of c times x cubed is three c times x squared. To match one half, c must be one sixth.

Continue the same rule. Each coefficient is the previous one divided by the next whole number. We get one, one, one half, one sixth, one twenty-fourth. Those denominators are factorials. As we add terms, watch the polynomial change on the same axes. These curves are partial sums, not yet the exact solution.

A finite polynomial cannot finish the job. Differentiation removes its highest power. With infinitely many terms, another term can supply each missing power. But dots are not a proof. We need to know that the sum exists and that differentiating it term by term is legitimate.

Choose any bounded interval, from minus R to R. The ratio of one absolute term to the previous one is at most R divided by its index. Eventually that ratio is at most one half. So the remaining terms fit beneath a shrinking geometric tail. The same argument works for the derivative series. Both converge uniformly on each bounded interval, which justifies differentiating term by term.

Call the sum E of x. The shifted coefficient rows now match all the way across: E prime equals E, and E of zero is one. We built a solution to our drawing rule. We still owe two explanations: why it is the only solution with that starting value, and why adding inputs should multiply outputs. The series gives us a way to answer both.
